::: {.lead-text}
Many problems in science and engineering are described by partial
differential equations (PDEs). Solving them accurately with high-fidelity
numerical methods is often very costly, which becomes prohibitive when the
same model must be run many times: for forecasting, optimization, control or
uncertainty quantification (UQ). My research develops reduced-order models
(ROMs) and surrogate models that make these computations fast while
preserving accuracy and the underlying physics.
:::

## ROMs in a nutshell

The solutions of a PDE often live, in practice, close to a space of much lower
dimension than the full numerical model. A ROM exploits this: it learns a small
set of representative modes from high-fidelity solutions, then describes any
new solution with only a few coefficients.

The computational effort is split into two stages:

- **Offline**, done once: high-fidelity simulations are computed and
  compressed into a reduced basis, for instance by Proper Orthogonal
  Decomposition (POD).
- **Online**, done many times: for a new parameter or scenario, only the few
  reduced coefficients are computed, which is orders of magnitude cheaper.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-align: center
flowchart LR
  A["Full-order model<br/>(PDE solver)"] --> B["Snapshots of<br/>the solution"]
  B --> C["Reduced basis<br/>(e.g. POD)"]
  C --> D["Intrusive:<br/>projection of the equations"]
  C --> E["Non-intrusive:<br/>learning from data"]
  D --> F["Fast online<br/>predictions"]
  E --> F
```

::: {.diagram-caption}
General principle of a ROM: a reduced basis is extracted offline, then the
reduced dynamics are obtained either by projecting the equations (intrusive)
or by learning them from data (non-intrusive).
:::

## Two families of approaches

::: {.research-grid}

::: {.research-card}
### <i class="bi bi-diagram-3"></i> Intrusive ROMs
The governing equations are projected onto the reduced basis (Galerkin-type
methods). This requires access to the operators of the numerical solver, but
keeps a direct link with the physics and allows error control.

Application: advection–diffusion problems.
:::

::: {.research-card}
### <i class="bi bi-cpu"></i> Non-intrusive ROMs
The reduced dynamics are learned directly from simulation data, for instance
with neural networks, without modifying the solver. This makes the approach
usable with existing, complex or industrial codes.

Application: 2D shallow-water equations and flood simulation.
:::

:::

## Application to floods

The two-dimensional shallow-water equations (SWE), also known as the
Saint-Venant equations, describe free-surface flows in rivers and floodplains.
They are central to flood forecasting, but their high-fidelity simulation is
costly, and the solutions are hard to reduce: the dynamics are nonlinear and
the wet/dry fronts move as the flood spreads.

My work builds non-intrusive ROMs for the 2D SWE that remain accurate on flood
scenarios not seen during training, follow moving flood fronts, and respect
physical quantities such as mass.

## Main contributions

My work has addressed several difficulties that make floods hard to reduce:

- **Accuracy with few modes.** By learning the POD projection error together
  with the reduced coefficients, the reduced model stays accurate with a small
  basis and compact neural networks, and was validated on real floods of the
  Aude river and the city of Abidjan.
- **Moving flood fronts.** Registering the moving wetted area onto a fixed
  domain, combined with a global water-volume constraint, captures advancing
  fronts with far fewer modes and much smaller errors.
- **Changing flow regimes.** Local ROMs, each adapted to a flow regime and
  selected online by a physics-guided classifier, improve accuracy when a
  single global model is not enough.
- **Speed for many-query studies.** The resulting surrogates simulate whole
  flood events in seconds, making large ensembles and uncertainty
  quantification affordable.

## Projects & collaborations

My PhD and my position as Teaching and Research Associate (2021–2026) were
carried out at the Institut de Mathématiques de Toulouse (IMT), INSA Toulouse.
During my PhD, I contributed to the ANR MUFFINS project, in
collaboration with INRAE, on efficient simulation and model reduction for
hydrodynamic applications.

I have worked with Jérôme Monnier (INSA Toulouse, IMT), Robin Bouclier (INSA
Toulouse, Institut Clément Ader) and Pierre-André Garambois (INRAE,
Aix-en-Provence).

## Looking ahead

I want to extend physics-guided, non-intrusive model reduction to broader
computational fluid dynamics. Directions I am particularly interested in:

- **Structure-preserving ROMs**: reduced models that retain the key
  properties of the original equations, such as conservation laws,
  stability or energy balance.
- **Parametric and unsteady flows**, with ROMs valid over wide ranges of
  physical parameters.
- **UQ**, where fast surrogates make large ensembles of simulations
  affordable.
- **Coupling numerical solvers with learned surrogates**, to combine the
  reliability of physics-based models with the speed of machine learning.

The common thread is ROMs that are fast, interpretable and reliable across
flow regimes.

Beyond hydrodynamics, I am open to applying ROMs to other fields where
high-fidelity simulations are a bottleneck, such as weather and climate
modeling, ocean and atmospheric flows, environmental engineering, energy
systems, or industrial fluid mechanics, and I welcome collaborations in these
areas.
